articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown Pensacola's Empty Storefronts: A Walking Tour of Palafox's Vacancies
articles.dek: Six months after two anchor tenants left Palafox Street, at least nine ground-floor retail spaces sit empty between Garden and Main. Property owners say rents haven't budged. Here's who owns what, what they're asking, and why the gaps persist.
brief: At least nine ground-floor retail spaces on Palafox Street between Garden and Main streets sit vacant, with asking rents ranging from $22 to $35 per square foot
Property owners representing six of the vacant storefronts confirmed they have not reduced asking rents despite spaces sitting empty for an average of 11 months
Downtown Improvement Board data shows foot traffic down 14% compared to the same period last year, though weekend numbers remain stable
articles.body:
The paper sign taped inside 24 S. Palafox has yellowed at the edges. "Coming Soon" it still reads, though the space has been empty since October. Through the dusty glass, you can see the outline where display cases once stood. A single extension cord snakes across the concrete floor to nowhere.

This is one of at least nine ground-floor retail vacancies on Palafox Street's commercial core, the five-block stretch between Garden and Main that serves as downtown Pensacola's economic backbone. Six months after the departures of Bodacious Bookshop and the Original Pensacola Trading Company—two tenants that together occupied nearly 6,000 square feet—the gaps remain unfilled.

A walking tour of the vacancies reveals a pattern: landlords holding firm on pre-pandemic rent expectations while prospective tenants balk at the numbers.

The Inventory

Starting at Garden Street and walking north, the first vacancy appears at 43 S. Palafox. The 1,800-square-foot corner space, previously a women's clothing boutique, has been empty for 14 months. Property records show the building is owned by Palafox Partners LLC, a holding company registered to a Destin address. A commercial listing through Beck Partners prices the space at $32 per square foot, triple net.

Half a block up, the former Bodacious Bookshop space at 33 S. Palafox remains dark. The 3,200-square-foot storefront anchored that block for 11 years before closing in December. Owner Sandra Weston, reached by phone, said she couldn't compete with online booksellers and a rent increase from $24 to $29 per square foot. The building's owner, Downtown Pensacola Properties Inc., has listed the space at $31 per square foot. Company principal Marcus Holt declined to comment on lease negotiations but confirmed no letters of intent are pending.

The pattern continues. At 24 S. Palafox, the "Coming Soon" sign marks what was supposed to be a craft cocktail bar. The business never opened. Escambia County property records show the building sold in March 2025 to an LLC registered in Birmingham. The new owners are asking $35 per square foot—the highest rate on the corridor.

Across the street, two adjacent spaces at 21 and 23 S. Palafox have been vacant since a gift shop consolidated into a smaller location on Intendencia. Combined, they offer 2,400 square feet. Listing agent Carla Simmons with Coldwell Banker Commercial said she's shown the spaces to "probably 30 prospective tenants" since February. Most walk away after seeing the rate: $28 per square foot.

"They do the math," Simmons said. "For 2,400 square feet at that rate, you're looking at $5,600 a month before utilities, insurance, any of it. A lot of small retailers just can't make those numbers work."

The Original Pensacola Trading Company Site

The most visible vacancy sits at 10 S. Palafox, where the Original Pensacola Trading Company operated for 23 years before closing in January. The 2,800-square-foot space occupies a prime corner with frontage on both Palafox and Intendencia. A large-format banner advertising the space now hangs where the store's iconic neon sign once glowed.

Former owner Dale Thornton, who still lives in East Hill, said the decision to close came down to economics. His rent had increased three times in five years, from $18 per square foot in 2021 to $26 in 2025. When his landlord proposed $30 for a new five-year lease, he calculated the numbers and couldn't make them work.

"We were a destination," Thornton said during an interview at his home. "People came downtown specifically to shop with us. But you can only sell so many T-shirts and shot glasses. The margin on tourist merchandise isn't what people think."

The building's owner, a trust administered through a Pensacola law firm, has listed the space at $29 per square foot. Attorney William Chen, who represents the trust, said the rate reflects "market conditions and the property's location advantages."

"This is the best corner on Palafox," Chen said. "The right tenant will recognize that value."

North of Romana

The vacancies thin out north of Romana Street, where older buildings give way to the Saenger Theatre block and newer mixed-use developments. But three more empty storefronts appear between Romana and Main.

At 118 N. Palafox, a narrow 900-square-foot space has been empty for eight months. The previous tenant, a vintage record shop, relocated to a less expensive spot on North Ninth Avenue. At 134 N. Palafox, a former art gallery closed in November after the owner retired. And at 156 N. Palafox, just south of Main, a 1,200-square-foot space has cycled through three tenants in four years. It's been empty since March.

Combined, these nine vacancies represent approximately 16,000 square feet of dormant retail space on Pensacola's most prominent commercial street.

The Numbers

Asking rents for the vacant Palafox spaces range from $22 to $35 per square foot, triple net. That pricing structure means tenants also pay property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs on top of base rent—typically adding $8 to $12 per square foot annually.

For context, retail spaces on Ninth Avenue in East Hill currently list between $16 and $22 per square foot. In Gulf Breeze's Harbourtown Shopping Village, rates run $18 to $24. Along Pensacola Beach's core commercial area, ground-floor retail ranges from $28 to $40 per square foot—but those spaces benefit from tourist foot traffic that downtown Pensacola cannot match.

Downtown Improvement Board Executive Director Lila Grant said the vacancy rate on Palafox between Garden and Main currently sits at approximately 12%, up from 7% in June 2025. She characterized the increase as "concerning but not alarming."

"We've been through cycles before," Grant said. "After 2008, we had vacancies over 20%. The market corrected. It will correct again."

DIB foot traffic data, collected through sensors at six intersections along Palafox, shows pedestrian counts down 14% compared to the same period last year. Weekend traffic has held relatively steady, Grant said, but weekday lunch-hour counts have dropped significantly.

"We're seeing fewer office workers downtown," she said. "Remote work changed those patterns and they haven't fully recovered."

Why Rents Haven't Moved

Property owners contacted for this story offered variations on the same explanation: they can afford to wait.

Marcus Holt, whose company owns the former Bodacious Bookshop building, said he's fielded interest from several potential tenants but hasn't found the right fit.

"I'm not desperate to fill the space," Holt said. "I'd rather wait for a tenant who will be there for 10 years than take the first person who walks in and watch them fail in 18 months."

Holt said he purchased the building in 2019 with cash and carries no mortgage. The property taxes on the three-story structure, which includes apartments above the retail space, run approximately $14,000 annually. Rental income from the upstairs units covers that and then some.

"The retail space is gravy," he said. "When the right tenant comes along at the right price, great. Until then, I'm fine."

This dynamic—property owners with low carrying costs holding out for premium rents—appeared repeatedly in conversations with landlords and commercial real estate agents.

Beth Armitage, a commercial broker with Studer Properties who is not involved in any of the current Palafox listings, said the pattern reflects broader shifts in downtown property ownership over the past decade.

"You had a lot of buildings change hands between 2015 and 2020," Armitage said. "Many of the new owners paid cash or put significant equity down. They're not leveraged the way previous owners were. That changes the calculus completely."

When a landlord has mortgage payments to make, an empty storefront bleeds money. When a landlord owns free and clear, an empty storefront is merely a missed opportunity—not a crisis.

What Prospective Tenants See

Three business owners who considered and rejected downtown Palafox locations agreed to speak on condition of anonymity, citing concerns about damaging relationships with property owners they might need to work with in the future.

One, who operates a successful café in another Pensacola neighborhood, said she spent four months exploring a Palafox space in early 2026. The asking rent was $27 per square foot for 1,600 square feet. With triple net charges, her total monthly occupancy cost would have exceeded $5,000.

"I ran the numbers six different ways," she said. "I would have needed to do $35,000 a month in sales just to break even. My current location does $28,000 on a good month, and I'm profitable because my rent is half that."

She said she offered the landlord $20 per square foot with annual escalators. The landlord declined.

Another prospective tenant, who owns a retail business in Gulf Breeze, said he was prepared to open a second location on Palafox but couldn't negotiate acceptable lease terms.

"The landlord wanted a five-year lease with personal guarantees," he said. "I offered three years with an option to renew. We couldn't get there."

The third, an entrepreneur planning a new concept, said she ultimately chose a location on Garden Street east of Palafox, where rents run approximately $18 per square foot.

"I wanted to be on Palafox," she said. "The foot traffic is better. But the rent difference was almost $2,000 a month. That's a full-time employee."

The City's Role

Pensacola City Council member Jennifer Patterson, whose District 6 includes downtown, said she's aware of concerns about Palafox vacancies but sees limited options for municipal intervention.

"We can't tell property owners what to charge for rent," Patterson said. "That's not how this works."

The city does offer incentive programs for downtown businesses, including facade improvement grants and a commercial rent subsidy pilot program launched in 2024. But the rent subsidy program, which provides up to $500 monthly for qualifying small businesses, has seen limited uptake. According to city records obtained through a public records request, only four businesses have received subsidies since the program began.

Patterson said she's asked city staff to examine whether vacant storefront regulations—ordinances that require property owners to maintain storefronts or face fines—might help address the issue. Several cities, including San Francisco and Detroit, have implemented such rules with mixed results.

"It's something we're looking at," Patterson said. "I'm not sure it's the right tool for Pensacola, but we're examining the options."

Mayor D.C. Reeves did not respond to requests for comment.

What Comes Next

Commercial real estate agents working the downtown market said they expect some landlords to adjust asking rents by fall if current spaces remain vacant.

"There's always a psychological threshold," said Beck Partners agent Tom Reilly. "For some owners, it's six months empty. For others, it's a year. But eventually most people start to move."

Reilly said he's seeing early signs of flexibility from some property owners, including willingness to offer tenant improvement allowances and shorter initial lease terms.

"Six months ago, nobody was talking about TI allowances downtown," he said. "Now I'm having those conversations. That tells me something."

For now, the storefronts remain empty. The paper signs promising "Coming Soon" continue to yellow in the windows. And the rents stay where they are, waiting for tenants who either haven't arrived or can't make the math work.

On a Tuesday afternoon last week, a woman stood outside the former Bodacious Bookshop space, shielding her eyes against the glass to peer inside. She studied the empty interior for a long moment, then moved on down the sidewalk.

No one followed her in.

articles.label: COUNTY GOVERNMENT
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1 Million No-Bid Contract With a Commissioner's Former Employer
articles.dek: Public records show the county awarded an emergency debris removal contract in April without competitive bidding to a firm where Commissioner Jeff Bergosh worked until 2019. County attorneys say it was legal. Ethics experts say it deserves scrutiny.
brief: Escambia County awarded a $2.1 million emergency debris removal contract to Gulf Coast Environmental Services in April without competitive bidding
Commissioner Jeff Bergosh worked as a project manager at GCES from 2014 to 2019 and abstained from the vote but participated in discussion
Florida ethics law prohibits officials from contracting with former employers for two years after leaving—Bergosh's departure was seven years ago
articles.body:
The contract landed on the county commission's consent agenda April 8, buried between a mosquito control agreement and a parks maintenance renewal. Item 7C: Emergency Debris Removal Services, Gulf Coast Environmental Services LLC, $2,147,500.

No discussion. No separate vote. The consent agenda passed 5-0 in under ninety seconds.

What the agenda item didn't mention: Gulf Coast Environmental Services employed Commissioner Jeff Bergosh for five years before he won his District 1 seat in 2020. Public records obtained by The Flightline through a records request show Bergosh worked as a project manager at GCES from March 2014 until August 2019, four months before he filed to run for commission.

Bergosh did not vote on the contract. Commission meeting minutes show he announced a conflict of interest and abstained before the consent agenda vote. But the minutes also show he participated in an earlier work session discussion about the county's debris removal needs—a discussion that preceded the contract award by three weeks.

"I don't see any legal issue here," County Attorney Alison Rogers said in an interview. "The commissioner properly abstained. Florida's ethics code has a two-year cooling off period for contracts with former employers. He left that company seven years ago."

The Emergency Declaration

The contract traces back to a March 15 severe weather event that dropped four inches of rain on northern Escambia County in two hours. Flooding damaged roads in the Cantonment area and toppled trees across a six-mile stretch of Highway 29.

County Administrator Wes Moreno declared a local emergency March 17, activating the county's authority to bypass normal procurement procedures. Under Florida Statute 252.38, counties can award contracts without competitive bidding during declared emergencies if the work relates directly to the emergency response.

But the debris removal contract wasn't awarded until April 8—twenty-two days after the emergency declaration and after most of the immediate storm damage had been cleared by county public works crews.

GCES began work April 14 in the Beulah area, according to county work orders. The scope expanded to include debris removal along Muscogee Road, Nine Mile Road and portions of unincorporated West Pensacola—areas that public works director Tom Chen acknowledged "weren't directly impacted by the March storm."

"We had a backlog," Chen said. "The emergency contract gave us flexibility to address debris issues that had accumulated over several months."

The Abstention Question

Bergosh declined an interview request but responded to questions via email.

"I followed the law and abstained from any vote involving my prior employer," Bergosh wrote. "I left GCES in 2019. There is no conflict. This is a non-story being pushed by political opponents."

Asked about his participation in the March work session discussion, Bergosh wrote: "Work sessions are informational. No votes occur. Commissioners discuss dozens of topics. I don't recall specifically discussing debris removal contracts."

Meeting recordings reviewed by The Flightline show Bergosh spoke three times during the work session's infrastructure portion on March 18. He asked Moreno about debris removal timelines, referenced "contractors I know who have capacity" and suggested the county "move quickly on procurement."

He did not mention GCES by name.

What Ethics Experts Say

Florida's ethics code—Section 112.313—prohibits public officials from having contractual relationships with businesses they were employed by within the preceding two years. Bergosh's seven-year gap puts him outside that window.

But the law also prohibits officials from using their position to give "special privilege" to former employers. That prohibition has no time limit.

"The statute is clear on the two-year rule, but the special privilege language is broader," said Robert Jarvis, a professor at Nova Southeastern University's law school who specializes in Florida government ethics. "The question isn't just whether he voted. It's whether he used his position to influence the process."

Jarvis reviewed the meeting records at The Flightline's request. He said Bergosh's work session comments "create an appearance issue even if they don't rise to a legal violation."

"When a commissioner talks about contractors they personally know in a meeting that leads to a no-bid contract for one of those contractors—that deserves scrutiny," Jarvis said. "It may be completely innocent. But this is exactly the kind of situation ethics disclosure laws are designed to illuminate."

Ben Wilcox, research director at the nonprofit watchdog group Integrity Florida, said the contract structure raises separate concerns.

"Emergency procurement is meant for emergencies," Wilcox said. "When you're awarding contracts three weeks later for work that isn't in the storm-impacted area, that's a stretch of the emergency authority. Add the former employer connection and you have the appearance of a workaround."

Gulf Coast Environmental Services

GCES is a Cantonment-based company that has held debris removal contracts with Escambia County since 2012. State corporate records show the company is owned by Marcus Webb, a Pensacola native who started the business in 2008.

Webb did not respond to phone calls or emails seeking comment.

The company has received $4.3 million in Escambia County contracts since 2020, according to county procurement records. The April contract is the first awarded under emergency provisions.

GCES also holds contracts with Santa Rosa County and the City of Milton. Neither municipality awarded GCES contracts during Bergosh's tenure at the company.

What Happens Next

Rogers, the county attorney, said no investigation is planned.

"The commissioner followed disclosure requirements," Rogers said. "Unless someone files a complaint with the state ethics commission, there's no mechanism for further review."

The Florida Commission on Ethics investigates complaints from citizens but does not initiate investigations on its own. Complaints must be sworn and filed within five years of the alleged violation.

Bergosh is up for reelection in 2024. He has filed paperwork indicating his intent to run and reported $47,000 in campaign contributions as of June 1.

The debris removal work under the GCES contract is scheduled to continue through August.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Summer Schedule Means 40 Practice Days Over Pensacola Beach Through August
articles.dek: The Navy's flight demonstration squadron returns to full practice tempo this week. For tourists, it's a free show. For year-round residents beneath the flight path, it's four months of jet noise starting at 11:30 a.m. A look at the schedule, the complaints, and what the Navy says about them.
brief: Blue Angels practice sessions run Tuesdays and Wednesdays through August, weather permitting, with 40 scheduled practice days over Pensacola Beach
Flight operations typically begin at 11:30 a.m. and last 45 to 60 minutes, with jets reaching noise levels up to 130 decibels during low passes
Naval Air Station Pensacola fields hundreds of noise complaints annually but says the practice location over the Gulf minimizes residential impact
articles.body:
The rumble starts before you see them. A low vibration in the chest, then the roar, then six F/A-18 Super Hornets in tight formation screaming over Via de Luna at 400 miles per hour.

It is 11:47 a.m. on a Tuesday in late June. Tourists on Pensacola Beach have stopped mid-stride, phones raised, necks craned. At the Margaritaville Beach Hotel, guests crowd the pool deck. A child covers his ears and grins.

Three blocks inland, in the Portofinito subdivision, Linda Hargrove closes her windows despite the heat.

"Every Tuesday and Wednesday from March to November," she said. "You learn to schedule your phone calls around it."

The Summer Schedule

The Blue Angels returned to their full practice tempo this week following a two-week road show swing through the Midwest. From now through late August, the squadron will conduct practice demonstrations over Pensacola Beach every Tuesday and Wednesday that weather permits.

That works out to approximately 40 practice days over the summer months, according to the squadron's published schedule on the Blue Angels website.

Practice sessions typically begin at 11:30 a.m. and run 45 to 60 minutes. The team performs the same maneuvers they execute at air shows across the country: the Diamond 360, the Opposing Knife Edge Pass, the Sneak Pass, the signature Delta formation.

The flight box—the designated airspace for maneuvers—sits over the Gulf of Mexico just off Pensacola Beach. The crowd line runs along the public beach near Portofino Island Resort. The Navy estimates 5,000 to 8,000 spectators gather on practice days during peak summer weeks.

There is no admission. No parking fee. No grandstand. Just sand, sun and supersonic noise.

The Noise Question

The F/A-18 Super Hornet produces up to 130 decibels during full afterburner passes. That is louder than a jackhammer at three feet. Louder than a thunderclap. The threshold for pain is 125 decibels.

Naval Air Station Pensacola maintains a noise complaint line and logs every call. Base spokesperson Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Foster said the installation received 847 noise complaints in fiscal year 2025, though she noted that figure includes all flight operations at NAS Pensacola, not just Blue Angels practices.

"The Blue Angels practice site was specifically chosen to minimize impact on residential areas," Foster said in an email. "By conducting demonstrations over the Gulf, we reduce the noise footprint over populated neighborhoods while still allowing public viewing access."

That explanation does not satisfy everyone who lives under the approach and departure paths.

Tom Kendrick has owned a home on Ariola Drive since 2011. He supports the military. He understands the economic value of the Blue Angels to Pensacola tourism. He also cannot hold a conversation in his backyard on practice days.

"I'm not saying they should stop," Kendrick said. "I'm saying maybe they don't need to do the same passes over the same streets forty times a summer. There's a whole Gulf out there."

The Economic Argument

The Navy and local tourism officials frame the practices as an economic engine.

Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm, does not break out Blue Angels-specific visitor data. But spokesperson Nicole Stacey said the squadron "remains one of our most recognized attractions" and that practice days show measurable upticks in beach parking revenue and restaurant traffic in the Pensacola Beach core.

The annual Pensacola Beach Air Show, held each July, draws an estimated 150,000 spectators over two days, according to event organizers. That event requires road closures, additional law enforcement, and coordination among Santa Rosa County, the Santa Rosa Island Authority and multiple federal agencies.

Tuesday practices require none of that. Spectators show up. The jets fly. Everyone goes home.

"It's the best free show in Florida," said Mark Thompson, general manager of the Hilton Pensacola Beach. "Our guests plan their trips around it."

What the Navy Says

The Blue Angels have called Pensacola home since 1949. The practice location over Pensacola Beach dates to the squadron's transition from Forrest Sherman Field to the current setup.

Foster, the NAS Pensacola spokesperson, said the Navy reviews its flight operations annually and considers community feedback as part of that process. She said there are no current plans to alter the practice schedule or location.

"The Blue Angels serve as ambassadors for the Navy and Marine Corps," Foster said. "The Pensacola community has supported this mission for decades, and we work hard to be good neighbors while maintaining the training standards our pilots need."

The squadron's published schedule shows practices continuing through November, with a reduced tempo in fall. The final home practice of the 2026 season is tentatively scheduled for November 11.

Until then, the jets will fly. The tourists will watch. And Linda Hargrove will close her windows.

"You get used to it," she said. "Mostly."
